backlog.spec: Let the data decide how many boosting rounds the LightGBM member needs instead of fixing 500. Inside fit_predict, split the training molecules by Murcko scaffold groups (MurckoScaffoldSmiles, falling back to the SMILES on failure) with GroupKFold(n_splits=5) and take one fold as a validation set; fit an LGBMRegressor with n_estimators=3000 and the current other hyperparameters using callbacks=[lightgbm.early_stopping(100, verbose=False)] against that validation set, read best_iteration_, then refit on all the training rows with n_estimators set to that value (scaled up by 5/4 to compensate for the held-out fifth, with a floor of 100 and a cap of 3000). Use the refit model's prediction as the LightGBM member exactly as before. The optimal number of rounds plausibly varies across the 15 folds, and a fixed 500 is either under- or over-fit depending on the fold; choosing it on scaffold-disjoint validation data matches how the harness evaluates.
backlog.title: Choose the LightGBM tree count by grouped early stopping

backlog.spec: Add a fourth feature block: 1024-bit Avalon counts from rdkit.Avalon.pyAvalonTools.GetAvalonCountFP, converted to a dense float32 array (iterate the nonzero elements of the returned sparse count vector into a zero array of length 1024). Place it between the ErG block and the Morgan count block in both the train and test hstack calls, so all three tree members see it; leave the Ridge member reading only the last N_BITS Morgan columns, unchanged. Avalon uses its own enumerated path and feature-class definitions rather than circular atom environments, so it encodes substructures that neither Morgan counts nor ErG pharmacophore shapes capture, and metabolic lability in hepatocytes is often driven by specific labile fragments. Keep every model, the rank target, and the 0.7/0.3 blend exactly as they are.
backlog.title: Add an Avalon count fingerprint block

backlog.spec: Before the log1p transform in the Ridge member, divide each molecule's Morgan count vector by its heavy-atom count (mol.GetNumHeavyAtoms(), floored at 1), then apply log1p. This removes the bias toward large molecules, whose counts are bigger, from the linear model's inputs. Use the same transform on training and test molecules. Keep Ridge alpha 10, the 0.7/0.3 blend and all tree members unchanged.
backlog.title: Size-normalized Morgan counts for the Ridge member

backlog.spec: Hold out a scaffold-grouped 15% of the training fold, using the Murcko scaffold of each training molecule as the group key, and train LightGBM and CatBoost with early stopping on this holdout (LightGBM: callbacks early_stopping(50) with a 1000-tree cap at learning_rate 0.03; CatBoost: early_stopping_rounds 50 with iterations 1500). Record the best iteration counts, then refit each booster on the full training fold with n_estimators or iterations set to 1.1 times the best count. Use the seed argument for the split and the models. The RF and Ridge members are unchanged.
backlog.title: Inner scaffold-grouped early stopping for boosters

backlog.spec: Hepatocyte clearance assays are noisy and a handful of mislabelled or unlearnable molecules can distort both the tree members and the Ridge. Inside fit_predict, before fitting the final models, run a single cheap inner pass: 5-fold KFold(shuffle=True, random_state=seed) over the training set with one LGBMRegressor (same hyperparameters as the existing member but n_estimators=300) to produce out-of-fold predictions of the rank target, compute absolute residuals, and drop the worst 5 percent of training rows. Then fit all four existing members (RF, LightGBM, CatBoost, Ridge) on the trimmed rows only, with the target re-ranked on the surviving subset, and keep the final 0.7/0.3 blend and all prediction-side code unchanged. The inner pass adds roughly one extra LightGBM fit per fold, well inside the time budget. The trim fraction is the single knob; keep it as a module-level constant TRIM_FRAC = 0.05 so a follow-up slot can test 0.10 or 0.02.
backlog.title: Trim high-residual training molecules via inner out-of-fold fits

backlog.spec: Replace the fixed Ridge(alpha=10.0) member with an alpha chosen inside fit_predict by scaffold-grouped cross-validation on the training set only. Compute Murcko scaffold strings for train_smiles with rdkit.Chem.Scaffolds.MurckoScaffold.MurckoScaffoldSmiles (fall back to the SMILES itself if it fails), use sklearn.model_selection.GroupKFold(n_splits=5) with those scaffolds as groups, and evaluate alpha in [1, 3, 10, 30, 100] on log1p of the Morgan count block, scoring each fold by Spearman correlation between predicted and true rank target (scipy.stats.spearmanr). Pick the alpha with the best mean fold score, refit Ridge with it on all the training rows, and use that prediction in place of the current pr. Keep the 0.7/0.3 blend, the rank target, and all three tree members untouched. This replaces a hand-set regularization constant with a data-driven one and should stabilize the linear member across folds where the fingerprint block is sparser.
backlog.title: Pick the Ridge alpha by scaffold-grouped inner CV

backlog.spec: Add a fourth member to the rank-averaged tree group: a second LGBMRegressor configured very differently from the first, using boosting_type='dart', n_estimators=600, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=63, colsample_bytree=0.6, subsample=0.7 with subsample_freq=1, min_child_samples=5, drop_rate=0.1, n_jobs=8, random_state=seed+1, verbose=-1. It is fitted on the same full feature matrix and the same rank target, its prediction is rank-normalized like the others, and it simply joins the mean over the models list so the 0.7/0.3 blend with the Ridge member is unchanged. The existing LightGBM is deliberately shallow and heavily column-subsampled; a deeper, less column-starved dart model makes different errors, and rank-averaging benefits mainly from decorrelated members rather than from individually better ones. Keep an eye on runtime: dart is slower, so reduce n_estimators if the job approaches the 10-minute limit.
backlog.title: Second LightGBM member with dart boosting for diversity

backlog.spec: Every featurizer in train.py calls Chem.MolFromSmiles(s) directly, so counterions, solvates, and multi-component SMILES contribute spurious atoms to the descriptors, ErG fingerprint, and Morgan counts. Add a single helper, e.g. def parse(s) that does m = Chem.MolFromSmiles(s); if m is None return a benzene fallback; otherwise split on fragments with Chem.GetMolFrags(m, asMols=True, sanitizeFrags=False) and keep the fragment with the most heavy atoms; then return that fragment. Route featurize, descriptors, and erg through parse instead of Chem.MolFromSmiles so all three feature blocks see the same cleaned molecule. This is a pure preprocessing change, about six lines, with no effect on model structure or runtime. It should mainly help the descriptor block, where MolWt, TPSA, and counts are badly distorted by salts, and the Ridge member, where counterion bits add noise to the log1p Morgan vector.
backlog.title: Strip salts and keep the largest fragment

backlog.spec: Add a correlation filter to the descriptor block so the tree members see fewer redundant columns. Inside fit_predict, after computing the raw descriptor matrix for the training molecules, standardize it, compute the absolute Pearson correlation matrix with numpy (guard against zero-variance columns by giving them correlation 0 and dropping them), and greedily drop any column whose absolute correlation with an already-kept column exceeds 0.95, walking columns in their original order. Apply the identical kept-column index list to the test descriptor matrix, then concatenate as before with ErG and Morgan counts. Do not change the models, the target, the Ridge member, or the ErG and Morgan blocks. RDKit's descList contains many nearly collinear variants (several molecular-weight, Chi, and Kappa flavours), which dilute the per-split feature sampling of the RF, LightGBM, and CatBoost members; removing them raises the chance each split sees an informative descriptor.
backlog.title: Prune near-duplicate RDKit descriptor columns

backlog.spec: The file already contains an unused minmax_kernel function. Replace the Ridge-on-log1p-Morgan member (the last four lines of fit_predict) with a KernelRidge member that uses the precomputed minmax Tanimoto kernel on the Morgan count block only: Ktr = minmax_kernel(Xtr[:, -N_BITS:], Xtr[:, -N_BITS:]), Kte = minmax_kernel(Xte[:, -N_BITS:], Xtr[:, -N_BITS:]), then KernelRidge(alpha=0.5, kernel='precomputed').fit(Ktr, y) and predict on Kte, rank-normalized and blended at the same 0.3 weight against 0.7 times the tree average. Note the distinction from the earlier rejected experiment: that one added kernel ridge as a fourth member inside the rank average, which diluted the trees; here kernel ridge replaces the linear member in the outer blend, occupying the slot of the model that is known to add the most value. Kernel ridge on this kernel was the strongest single model earlier in the run, so it is a natural substitute for Ridge in the outer blend.
backlog.title: Swap the Ridge member for minmax-Tanimoto kernel ridge

backlog.spec: Fit each of the RF, LightGBM and CatBoost members 3 times with seeds seed, seed+1 and seed+2. Average the 3 predictions of each member before ranking. Keep the hyperparameters the same. This reduces variance, and the run time should stay within 10 minutes.
backlog.title: Seed-bagged tree members

backlog.spec: Change the existing LGBMRegressor member to objective='regression_l1' (MAE) while keeping all its other hyperparameters identical: 500 trees, learning_rate 0.03, 15 leaves, colsample_bytree 0.3, subsample 0.8 with subsample_freq 1, min_child_samples 10. Nothing else changes: same features, same uniform rank target, same per-member rank normalization, same 0.7/0.3 blend with the Ridge member. On a bounded uniform rank target the squared-error objective spends much of its capacity chasing molecules at the extremes of the rank scale, whereas an L1 objective fits the conditional median and is far less sensitive to the handful of molecules whose scaffold-held-out rank is badly mispredicted. Because the final score is Spearman, only the ordering matters, so a median-style fit is well matched to the metric.
backlog.title: Switch the LightGBM member to an L1 objective

backlog.spec: Add a helper mol(s) that parses SMILES with Chem.MolFromSmiles, then keeps the largest fragment by heavy atom count using rdkit.Chem.rdmolops.GetMolFrags(m, asMols=True) and max by GetNumHeavyAtoms. Use it in featurize, descriptors and erg instead of calling Chem.MolFromSmiles directly. Leave the rest unchanged.
backlog.title: Strip salts, keep largest fragment

backlog.spec: Inside fit_predict, fit a quick RF (100 trees) on Xtr with 5-fold out-of-fold predictions. Remove the 5% of training molecules with the largest absolute rank residual. Then fit all members on the cleaned set. Use KFold with shuffle and the seed.
backlog.title: Drop high-residual training molecules

backlog.spec: Add count Avalon fingerprints (rdkit.Avalon.pyAvalonTools.GetAvalonCountFP with nBits=1024, converted to a numpy array) to the Ridge member's input, concatenated with log1p Morgan counts. Tree members keep their current features. Use the same Ridge alpha.
backlog.title: Avalon fingerprint block for Ridge

backlog.spec: In fit_predict, change the Ridge member: use Ridge(alpha=3.0) on log1p Morgan counts, and change the final blend to 0.6*np.mean(preds,axis=0) + 0.4*rankdata(pr)/len(pr). Nothing else changes.
backlog.title: Ridge blend weight 0.4, alpha 3

backlog.spec: Replace np.mean(preds,axis=0) with the weighted sum 0.25*RF + 0.375*LGBM + 0.375*CatBoost, using the already rank-normalized predictions. Keep the Ridge blend at 0.3.
backlog.title: Rank-average weight toward LightGBM/CatBoost

backlog.spec: Simplify the rank-averaged part of the ensemble from three members to two by deleting the CatBoostRegressor entry from the models list (and its import), so the 0.7 weight is split between the RandomForestRegressor and the LGBMRegressor only. Leave everything else exactly as it is: the same features, the same rank target, the same per-member rank normalization, and the same 0.7/0.3 blend with the Ridge member on log1p Morgan counts. CatBoost was added in slot 29 and measured 0.4745, identical to the incumbent, so it may be contributing nothing but runtime and code. If the loss stays within noise of the incumbent, the simpler and much faster two-member ensemble should be preferred on its own merits and leaves more headroom in the 10-minute budget for future members.
backlog.title: Drop the CatBoost member and keep RF plus LightGBM

backlog.spec: Bin the training rank target into 8 equal-frequency classes (np.digitize on quantiles of y). Fit an LGBMRegressor-style LGBMClassifier with objective multiclass, 300 trees, learning rate 0.05, num_leaves 15, colsample_bytree 0.3, subsample 0.8 and subsample_freq 1, using the same feature matrix Xtr. At prediction time, score each test molecule as the probability-weighted mean of the class midpoints (values in (0,1)). Rank-normalize this score and add it as a fifth member to the existing rank average of the RF, LightGBM and CatBoost members, keeping the 0.7/0.3 split with the Ridge unchanged.
backlog.title: Ordinal multiclass LightGBM as a fifth rank member

backlog.spec: In fit_predict, the final line blends the rank-averaged tree ensemble and the Ridge member as 0.7 * tree_mean + 0.3 * ridge_rank. The Ridge member was the single largest recent win (0.4922/0.4939, replicated), which suggests the linear model on log1p Morgan counts carries information the trees miss and may currently be underweighted. Change the blend to 0.55 * tree_mean + 0.45 * ridge_rank and at the same time lower the Ridge regularization from alpha=10.0 to alpha=3.0. Keep everything else identical: same features, same rank target, same three tree members, same rankdata normalization of each prediction vector. This is a two-number change on existing lines, so it costs nothing in runtime or code complexity, and it probes the most promising direction left in the current architecture. If it helps, a follow-up slot can bracket the weight further (0.5 vs 0.4); if it hurts, the incumbent 0.7/0.3 split is confirmed as near-optimal.
backlog.title: Tune the Ridge blend weight and alpha

memo:
Helped: target handling and, above all, ensembling diverse members. The rank target gave 0.5286/0.5252 (replicated). The rank-averaged RF+LightGBM+kernel ensemble reached 0.5083. A 30% Ridge member on log1p Morgan counts gave 0.4922/0.4939 (replicated). ErG pharmacophore features gave the incumbent, 0.4745 (1 run only, a 0.0186 gain, about 2.7 noise sd).
Did not help: single tree models (ExtraTrees 0.6287/0.5571, RF 0.5564, LightGBM 0.5442), SVR 0.5699, MLP 0.5515, scaffold weights 0.5477, Gaussian quantile target 0.5289. Recent additions were flat or worse: CatBoost 0.4745, kernel ridge member 0.4787, atom-pair counts 0.4777, kNN 0.4812, NNLS blend 0.4782, torsion counts 0.4739, RF tweaks 0.4768/0.4743. All of these are within noise (sd 0.0070).
Next: replicate ErG first. Then tune the Ridge blend weight and alpha, and try other feature blocks such as MACCS. Read train.py before writing specs, since several slots were lost to aborts.
